evidence.exact_quote: Before any permission match, path comparison, or scope check, paths MUST be normalized in this order:
`realpath()` failure is fail-closed. Broken symlink, permission error, or missing target means deny.

items.impact: This is a concrete fail-closed security contract: unresolved or noncanonical paths cannot fall back to permissive matching.
items.statement: Path permission checks have an explicit normalization order and deny on canonicalization failure.
items.title: Canonical path matching is fail closed

evidence.exact_quote: Permission rules are evaluated in a strict layer precedence. The first layer that produces a defined rule for the invocation wins; higher-precedence layers shadow lower layers on a per-rule basis, but they do NOT replace the entire lower ruleset.
when requested and effective state differ, the effective state is what executes

items.impact: Implementations and GUI consumers have a common authority model and must expose clamps rather than implying unavailable capability.
items.statement: The SSOT defines layered rule precedence, downward-only child inheritance, scope specificity, and requested-versus-effective disclosure.
items.title: Layered authority and effective-state disclosure are explicit

evidence.exact_quote: Resolve symlinks with `realpath()`; this is the symlink-root canonicalization step.
Match only against the normalized canonical path.

items.impact: A permitted target can be swapped after `realpath()` and before open or dispatch, allowing a time-of-check/time-of-use escape despite correct initial matching.
items.statement: The normalization contract does not bind the approved canonical object to the object actually opened, nor require descriptor-relative execution or a final identity recheck.
items.title: Path checks leave a TOCTOU substitution gap

evidence.exact_quote: Define `approval_scope_key` across actor/lane/run/account context and require reuse across permissions, HITL, doom-loop, and session approval caching.
the explicit `/actor/lane` scope key includes actor, run, lane, account, and package/seam context before approval reuse

items.impact: Different callers can serialize the same scope differently or omit a dimension, producing false cache misses or unsafe approval reuse across parallel actors, lanes, accounts, packages, or seams.
items.statement: The scope dimensions are named, but the key's canonical field set, ordering, null treatment, escaping, versioning, and equality algorithm are not defined.
items.title: Approval scope key has no canonical encoding

evidence.exact_quote: Provider route credentials, OAuth/session state, API keys, subscription-backed auth, authorization URLs, local account roots, and provider-native tool access are governed by PM permission custody and secret redaction.
Provider-native tool access goes through permission snapshots and redaction profiles.

items.impact: Provider routes cannot use discovery or provider-native access as a secret-custody or permission bypass.

items.title: Provider route secret custody is explicit

evidence.exact_quote: Plans, ledgers, logs, runtime artifacts, usage rows, and GUI diagnostics may store credential locators, account/profile refs, redacted setup state, and proof metadata, but never raw secrets.

items.impact: Storage and UI implementers cannot tell whether canonical account/profile references are allowed metadata or forbidden account identifiers, causing either loss of required joins or privacy leakage.

items.title: Allowed account refs conflict with forbidden identifiers

segments.summary: Reviewed SSOT scope, account/approval reconciliation, normalization, authority layers, permission actions, scope specificity, requested/effective disclosure, granular matching, and provider addendum boundary; found TOCTOU and approval-scope-key encoding gaps.

Reviewed PS-119 custody, case matching, external directories, durable suggestions, web key/egress/approval behavior, guards, presets, ask recovery, defaults, resolution, banned commands, hook rechecks, and shell boundary; found secret-category, host-scope, approval-transition, and batch-contract defects.

Reviewed cleanup gating, durable and projected storage, GUI disclosure/editors/presets/scopes, security model, audit, baseline, acceptance criteria, publication addendum, and blocked-outcome entry; found invalid TOML, rule identity oracle omission, projection lifecycle ambiguity, and preset divergence.

Reviewed blocked payload families, domain approvals, dedupe/revalidation, uncertain remote outcomes, snapshot schema and lifecycle, wakeup, target-bound preflight, provider exposure and residue cleanup, ownership, and PS-002 through PS-004; found enum, ordering, and acceptance-oracle defects.

Reviewed PS-005 through PS-011 actor/lane scope, execution snapshots, artifact hooks, action identity, remote-side-effect authority, provider disclosure, and projection health; found non-product oracles, under-bound graph identity, and GUI classification errors.

Reviewed PS-012 through PS-018 route facts, compact surfaces, path safety, HTE/DAE, locking and hook rechecks, executable trust, and enterprise host outcomes with PS-019 context; found missing runtime oracles, DAE failure containment, immutable executable binding, outcome precedence, and accessibility/localization bounds.
